fixes.answer: I think it is largely driven by social media, which has made fame appear both [[glamorous]] and easily attainable. Young people see influencers achieving wealth and adoration seemingly overnight, which is highly [[seductive]]. There is also a deeper human desire for validation and significance. Unfortunately, this often means chasing fame as an end in itself rather than as a [[by-product]] of genuine achievement.

The effects are often [[detrimental]], in my view. Constant exposure to celebrities' curated, idealised lives can create unrealistic expectations and [[fuel insecurity]], especially about appearance. It can also promote materialism and a distorted sense of what matters. That said, positive celebrities who [[champion]] good causes can be a genuinely inspiring influence, so it is not entirely negative.
fixes.why: 'fuel' is part of a collocation, 'inspiring' is plain; marked 'fuel insecurity' and 'champion'

fixes.answer: I would argue they do, whether they like it or not. Given the enormous influence they [[wield]] over millions of impressionable fans, celebrities have a certain moral [[obligation]] to behave responsibly. Their actions can genuinely shape public attitudes. However, it is also unfair to expect them to be flawless, since they are human. The key is a basic level of [[accountability]] and awareness.

I [[have some sympathy with]] that view. It does seem [[disproportionate]] that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels [[morally questionable]], it is economically logical.
fixes.why: 'logical' is plain; marked 'have some sympathy with' and the collocation 'morally questionable'
